effect_estimate.comment: Exact ITT estimates from Tables 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 combining administrative utility billing records and 9-month follow-up surveys.
effect_estimate.value: (1) Face-to-face tenant engagement RCT (N = 2,584 compounds): null effect on making at least one payment within 1 month (ITT = -0.005, SE = 0.018, p = 0.776; control mean = 0.301) or 9 months (ITT = -0.002, SE = 0.019, p = 0.928; control mean = 0.558), total amount paid within 1 month (US$ 0.049, SE = 0.642, p = 0.939) or 9 months (US$ -0.575, SE = 2.011, p = 0.775), and proportion of balance paid within 1 month (0.013, SE = 0.017, p = 0.436) or 9 months (0.008, SE = 0.015, p = 0.616). (2) Targeted contract enforcement / disconnection notices cluster-RCT (N = 1,001 disconnection-eligible compounds in 142 street clusters): increased probability of making at least one payment by 30.0 percentage points within 1 month (ITT = 0.300, SE = 0.039, p < 0.001; control mean = 0.110) and 19.5 percentage points within 9 months (ITT = 0.195, SE = 0.043, p < 0.001; control mean = 0.334); increased total amount paid by US$ 8.783 within 1 month (SE = 1.714, p < 0.001; control mean = US$ 5.026) and US$ 9.078 within 9 months (SE = 4.154, p = 0.031; control mean = US$ 24.722); and increased proportion of balance paid by 11.3 percentage points within 1 month (ITT = 0.113, SE = 0.025, p < 0.001; control mean = 0.268) and 7.8 percentage points within 9 months (ITT = 0.078, SE = 0.027, p = 0.005; control mean = 0.300), with no significant within-cluster spillovers (N = 996 eligible and N = 1,930 ineligible compounds). (3) Water/sanitation access and social/rental outcomes at 9 months: 96 compounds (2.9% of 3,253 accounts) were disconnected and most were quickly reconnected after agreeing to payment plans, resulting in no significant effects at 9 months on compound piped water connection (ITT = -0.036, SE = 0.024, p = 0.135, N = 600; control mean = 0.916), working piped water connection (ITT = -0.033, SE = 0.041, p = 0.423, N = 591; control mean = 0.573), pour-flush toilet connection (ITT = -0.014, SE = 0.019, p = 0.471, N = 608; control mean = 0.942), piped water as main source (ITT = 0.040, SE = 0.037, p = 0.286, N = 589), metered consumption (ITT = 2.583, SE = 20.684, p = 0.901, N = 474), monthly household water spending (US$ 0.664, SE = 1.005, p = 0.509, N = 334), perceived fairness/quality, or monthly tenant rent (US$ -1.845, SE = 2.576, p = 0.474, N = 395), while property owners offset costs by increasing the share of compounds renting out dwellings (+13.5 percentage points, ITT = 0.135, SE = 0.038, p < 0.001, N = 568) and monthly compound rental income (+US$ 23.880, SE = 10.127, p = 0.019, N = 525; control mean = US$ 62.575).

mechanism_flags.comment: The paper examines contract enforcement of utility service disconnection for nonpayment and loan arrears (disconnection, sanction, reconnection without enforcing formal reconnection fees upon cooperating), financial hardship exemptions and flexible payment plans (hardship_exception, accommodation), bill dispute channels and tenant complaints (administrative_review, complaint), prior ad hoc vs. targeted rule-bound enforcement (discretion), subsidized connection loans and monthly water/sewer tariffs (fees), utility CDA outreach and meter/billing assistance (bureaucratic_assistance), tenant bottom-up accountability and community committees (participation), and landlord/property-owner vs. tenant and resident/non-resident ownership dynamics (tenure, property).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The primary contract enforcement (disconnection notice) experiment evaluating payment and water/sanitation access outcomes was randomized at the street-cluster level across 147 street clusters (two-stage cluster randomization), matching RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant). Note that the sequential engagement arm was individually randomized across 2,584 tenant-occupied compounds.

sample_size.comment: Reports baseline listing sample (5,091 accounts), engagement RCT sample (2,584 accounts), enforcement cluster-RCT frame (3,253 accounts in 147 street clusters) and analytic samples (1,001 disconnection-eligible compounds in 142 clusters for direct ITT; 996 eligible and 1,930 ineligible compounds for spillovers), and 9-month endline survey samples (up to 608 compounds/owners and 403 tenants), as well as 2015/2016 Kayole Soweto baseline descriptive surveys (up to 3,327 utility billing accounts, 2,287 owners, and 4,178 tenants in Tables 1-2).
sample_size.value: 5,091 property owners / compound accounts across 6 informal settlements (August 2018 phone listing survey); 2,584 tenant-occupied compound accounts across 6 settlements in engagement RCT (1,292 treatment, 1,292 control); 3,253 compound accounts in 147 street clusters across 4 settlements in enforcement cluster-RCT (direct ITT payment analysis: 1,001 disconnection-eligible compounds in 142 clusters [327 treatment, 674 pure control]; spillover analysis: 996 eligible compounds in 144 clusters [322 spillover control, 674 pure control] and 1,930 ineligible compounds in 143 clusters; 9-month follow-up survey: up to 608 compounds / property owners and 403 tenants)

study_design.comment: Authors report two sequential field experiments (AEARCTR-0003556) combining 5 years of administrative utility billing data with baseline and 9-month endline surveys of property owners and tenants, plus baseline descriptive/OLS correlate analysis (Table 3).
study_design.value: Two sequential randomized controlled field experiments: (1) an individually randomized controlled trial of face-to-face tenant engagement and (2) a two-stage street-level cluster-randomized controlled trial of contract enforcement via targeted disconnection notices, analyzed with intention-to-treat (ITT) regressions with settlement fixed effects using administrative billing data and follow-up property owner and tenant surveys
